newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-India aluminium industry seen picking up.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-India aluminium industry seen picking up.

text.p: India's aluminium sector, saddled with inventories after a dip in domestic demand, is expected to pick up following positive signs in the economy, a senior industry official said on Tuesday.

"1996/97 (April-March) has been a less than expected year for the industry as (metal) prices came down because of dropping LME (London Metal Exchange) prices, the cost push imposed by the government on oil, coal, power...and recession in the last two quarters," said Rana M. Philip, deputy managing director of the Indian Aluminium Company Ltd (INDAL).
Philip told Reuters in an interview that the aluminium industry should see a turnaround in the new financial year beginning on April 1.
"In 1997/98, we expect it to pick up because agriculture income has been good in 1996/97, positive signs in the budget and more liberal credit policies," Philip said.

INDAL, the largest manufacturer of finished aluminium products in the country, annually produces over 50,000 tonnes of aluminium and buys about 30,000 tonnes. It earned a net profit of 1.15 billion rupees ($32 million) in 1995/96.
INDAL is 34.6 percent owned by Canada's Alcan Aluminium.
India has an annual production capacity of 610,000 tonnes of aluminium metal but output is much lower. It annually consumes around 500,000 tonnes of metal.
Industry officials said domestic aluminium producers had around April last year delinked their prices from LME prices, which had begun to drop.
The domestic fabricating industry preferred to import the metal at cheaper prices rather than buy it locally and domestic producers were unable to liquidate stocks.
Aluminium prices on the LME hit a two-year low in mid-October to around $1,300 per tonne.
Philip said Indian aluminium producers currently held about 20,000-30,000 of excess inventories, over and above the normal inventory of about 30,000 tonnes.
He said according to present indications the LME prices of the metal were moving up and ruling around $1600 per tonne.
"If this trend remains then the coming quarter should be better," Philip said.
He said the demand growth for aluminium in the country in 1996/97 had dropped to about two percent compared to an average eight percent.

Philip said in the last five months of the current fiscal year cement, paper and steel sectors were carrying a lot of inventories and the auto industry too was beginning to feel the pinch in the last quarter. "But if the growth picks up with more infrastructure investments and improvement in the capital market then 1997/98 should be better," he said.
Industry officials said falling orders for rolled products from the transport sector and spending cuts in the electricty sector, which uses wire rods, had contributed to the lower demand.
"The government is talking about more investment-friendly budget and metal prices are moving up in the international market, 1997/98 should be better," Philip said.

V. Raghuraman, secretary general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters the growth of the aluminium industry would depend to a large extent on the government's plans in the coming years.
"It will depend on the government spending because government is a major buyer," Raghuraman said. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
